description: We are Team Nokhottro (নক্ষত্র, “star”): Fariya Hossain, Mehbuba Uddin and Ishadi Kabir Protha, three friends who teamed up online from different countries to make NASA’s history an adventure for young explorers. For the Abandoned but not Forgotten challenge, we created Space Junk: The Great Space Mess!, a 7-minute animated episode where Spark, a little spacecraft, meets the Moon, Mars and the real NASA hardware left behind, and learns why we must keep Earth’s orbit clean. ✨
summary: Project Nokhottro is a 7-minute animated cartoon episode, “Space Junk: The Great Space Mess!”, that introduces school-age space enthusiasts to the real hardware NASA has left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space, and the science it made possible. Kids follow Spark, a young spacecraft, as Moony (the Moon) and Marsy (Mars) proudly show off historic explorers like Apollo 11’s Eagle, the Lunar Roving Vehicles, Viking, Spirit, Opportunity and Ingenuity, before the story explains how these monuments differ from the dangerous debris crowding Earth’s orbit. Built entirely in code and playable in any web browser with voices, subtitles and music, it helps young explorers learn space history and why we must keep space clean for future missions.
details:
What it does
Project Nokhottro is a 7-minute animated cartoon episode, "Space Junk: The Great Space Mess!", for school-age space fans (about ages 9–14). Spark, a cheerful young spacecraft, launches into space, says goodbye to the rocket stages that carried it, and meets Moony (the Moon) and Marsy (Mars). Each of them proudly shows off the real NASA hardware left on their surface. Every piece has a "museum" name tag: on the Moon, the Surveyor landers, Apollo 11's Eagle descent stage, the Lunar Roving Vehicles and ALSEP; on Mars, Viking 1 and 2, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight and Ingenuity. A deep-space montage then shows Dawn at Ceres, NEAR Shoemaker on Eros, Kepler trailing Earth, and Pioneer 10 and 11 leaving the Solar System.

How it works
The whole episode is drawn and animated in code. It runs in any web browser from one HTML file hosted on GitHub Pages, with no installation or login. It has character voices, subtitles, background music, sound effects, scene transitions, a scene selector, and a button that records the episode as a video file.

Benefits and intended impact
The episode teaches children what NASA left behind and the science each mission made possible. It also explains an important difference: retired hardware on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space are historic monuments, while the dangerous "space junk" is the debris crowding Earth's orbit. It shows three real problems (collisions, danger to astronauts, and risks to future missions) and ends with solutions (tracking debris, designing satellites that can be safely disposed of, and removing dangerous objects). We want young viewers to feel proud of space exploration and responsible for keeping space usable for their generation.

Tools and languages

  • HTML5 Canvas and JavaScript for all characters, NASA hardware drawings and animation
  • Web Audio API for music and sound effects generated in code
  • Web Speech API, plus Python with the edge-tts library, for character voices (Microsoft neural text-to-speech)
  • MediaRecorder API for exporting the episode as video
  • Visual Studio Code, GitHub and GitHub Pages for development and hosting
  • PowerPoint for our presentation
  • Claude (AI) assisted with coding, fact-checking and writing

How it is creative
Instead of a lecture, we turned NASA history into a story with personalities. The Moon is a proud "celebrity" with a crown, Mars gets jealous until her own visitors arrive, and the rocket stages are siblings cheering Spark on. Real hardware appears as respected exhibits in a space museum, which makes facts memorable and fun.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific accuracy, checked against NASA mission pages
  • Age-appropriate language and humour
  • Keeping a clear line between historic artifacts and harmful debris
  • Accessibility: subtitles, adjustable voices, and playback in a browser on any device
  • Keeping the runtime to about 7 minutes to hold attention

What we achieved and learned: We completed a full 7-minute episode across 8 scenes, published it online with GitHub Pages, and tested it in different browsers. We found that Microsoft Edge gives the most natural character voices, and we checked every fact about the NASA hardware against official NASA mission pages. We learned how much hardware NASA has left across the solar system, and why historic artifacts and orbital debris are very different things.
